findings.claim: Martial ends the poem with a complaint: cur sine te ceno, cum tecum, Pontice, cenem? — why do I dine without you, although I am dining with you, Ponticus?
findings.problem: The quotation is verbatim, but it is line 9 of the ten-line epigram, not the ending. In the prescribed booklet (and the Latin text of Epigrams 3.60) the poem closes with the following line, 'sportula quod non est, prosit: edamus idem.' The accompanying revision tip compounds the error by asking students to recall this line as 'the final line'.
findings.correction: Martial's penultimate line makes the complaint explicit: cur sine te ceno, cum tecum, Pontice, cenem? — why do I dine without you, although I am dining with you, Ponticus? — before the poem closes with sportula quod non est, prosit: edamus idem — since there is no dole, let it be of benefit: let us eat the same. (Revision tip: 'Close this and recall the closing couplet of Martial's epigram from memory — what is the speaker really complaining about?')

findings.claim: The poem lists pairs of foods, one line for the host’s dish and the next for the speaker’s inferior version
findings.problem: The prescribed text does not use that arrangement throughout: in lines 5 and 6 both the host's dish and the speaker's substitute stand within a single line ('sunt tibi boleti, fungos ego sumo suillos'; 'res tibi cum rhombo est, at mihi cum sparulo'), while only lines 3-4 and 7-8 split the pair across two lines.
findings.correction: The poem works through paired dishes — sometimes a line for the host's dish and the next for the speaker's inferior version, sometimes both halves of the pair packed into a single line (sunt tibi boleti, fungos ego sumo suillos)

findings.claim: Apollo tells Octavian that the sea, not just the land, is already his: vince mari: iam terra tua est — conquer at sea, the land is yours already.
findings.problem: The framing sentence inverts the meaning of the prescribed line. In the source text (Propertius, Elegy 4.6, 'vince mari: iam terra tua est') Apollo says the LAND is already Octavian's and orders him to go on and win the SEA — the sea is precisely what has not yet been won. The supplied gloss is correct, but the sentence introducing it contradicts it, and a student repeating it would misread the line.
findings.correction: Apollo tells Octavian that the land is already his and urges him now to win the sea as well: vince mari: iam terra tua est — conquer at sea, the land is yours already.

findings.claim: Much earlier in the same poem, Propertius recalls how Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome, watched the flight of birds as an <dfn>augur</dfn> before building the city’s walls
findings.problem: Speaker and location are both wrong against the source booklet. The Romulus/augur reference ('quam nisi defendes, murorum Romulus augur / ire Palatinas non bene vidit aves') is spoken by Apollo inside the prescribed lines (Elegy 4.6.43-44), only a few couplets before the Caesar line quoted above it — not by Propertius in narration, and not 'much earlier in the same poem'. It is also a warning (Romulus watched the birds in vain unless Octavian defends Rome), not a neutral recollection.
findings.correction: A few lines earlier in the same speech, Apollo warns that unless Octavian defends his country, Romulus — the legendary founder of Rome and <dfn>augur</dfn> of its walls — watched the flight of the birds over the Palatine in vain — another example of a Roman leader whose authority rested on a sign from the gods.

findings.claim: The poem ends with the deified spirit of Julius Caesar watching from the stars and declaring his own divinity
findings.problem: Elegy 4.6 runs to 86 lines and continues after line 60 with the poet's celebration of the Actian victory; line 60 ('sum deus; est nostri sanguinis ista fides') is the end of the prescribed extract, not the end of the poem.
findings.correction: The prescribed extract ends with the deified spirit of Julius Caesar watching from the stars and declaring his own divinity

findings.claim: Cicero delivered fourteen speeches attacking Mark Antony after the assassination of Julius Caesar in 44 BC.
findings.problem: Fourteen Philippics survive, but the Second Philippic — the speech studied here — was never actually delivered; it was written as though addressed to the senate and circulated in writing in late 44 BC (Dickinson College Commentaries; standard scholarship on the Philippics). The lesson itself later says Cicero 'composed' it.
findings.correction: Cicero wrote fourteen speeches attacking Mark Antony after the assassination of Julius Caesar in 44 BC; the second of them, studied here, was circulated in writing rather than actually delivered.

findings.claim: These speeches are called <dfn>Philippics</dfn>, after speeches once given against a Greek tyrant.
findings.problem: Demosthenes' Philippics attacked Philip II, king of Macedon, not a 'Greek tyrant'. The lesson's own glossary entry for 'Philippic' states this correctly, so the body text contradicts it.
findings.correction: These speeches are called <dfn>Philippics</dfn>, after the speeches the Athenian orator Demosthenes gave against Philip II, king of Macedon.

findings.claim: psallere et saltare — “to play music and to dance” — and posse versus facere, iocum movere — “to be able to compose poetry, to make a joke” — are historic infinitives
findings.problem: Wrong grammatical label for psallere and saltare. In the set text (Bellum Catilinae 25, prescribed booklet) the words are 'psallere et saltare poterat elegantius quam necesse est probae': both infinitives are complementary (prolative) infinitives governed by the finite verb poterat, not historic infinitives. Only in the later clause 'verum ingenium eius haud absurdum: posse versus facere, iocum movere, sermone uti...' are posse, movere and uti historic infinitives (facere there depends on posse). A student who copies this label will misidentify the construction in a grammar or style answer.
findings.correction: Notice the grammar Sallust chooses for these accomplishments. In psallere et saltare poterat — “she could play music and dance” — the two infinitives simply complete the verb poterat. Later, however, Sallust drops the finite verbs altogether: posse versus facere, iocum movere, sermone uti — “she could compose poetry, make a joke, use language…” — where posse, movere and uti are historic infinitives, a form used for rapid, repeated action in the past. Sallust piles these up quickly, giving the impression of a long list of talents rehearsed almost too smoothly.

findings.claim: {"q": "What grammatical form are 'psallere' and 'saltare' in Sallust's description?", "a": "Historic infinitives, showing habitual past action."}
findings.problem: Factually wrong. In Bellum Catilinae 25 the phrase is 'psallere et saltare poterat': the infinitives are complementary/prolative, depending on the finite verb poterat. The historic infinitives in this passage are posse, movere and uti in 'posse versus facere, iocum movere, sermone uti'.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which infinitives in Sallust's sketch of Sempronia are historic infinitives, and which merely complete a finite verb?", "a": "posse, movere and uti are historic infinitives; psallere and saltare simply complete poterat."}

findings.claim: In Sallust's phrases 'psallere et saltare poterat' and 'posse versus facere, iocum movere', identify the grammatical form used for psallere, saltare, facere and movere, and explain what effect this form creates. ... Mastering: Correctly identifies the historic infinitive and explains clearly how it conveys repeated, habitual past action
findings.problem: The question and its mark scheme require students to call all four infinitives historic infinitives. In the set text psallere and saltare depend on poterat (complementary infinitives) and facere depends on posse; only posse, movere (and uti) are historic infinitives. The 'correct' answer demanded is grammatically wrong.
findings.correction: In Sallust's phrase 'posse versus facere, iocum movere, sermone uti', identify the grammatical form of posse, movere and uti, explain what effect this form creates, and say how it differs from the infinitives in 'psallere et saltare poterat'. || Mastering: Correctly identifies posse, movere and uti as historic infinitives and explains how they convey rapid, repeated past action, while recognising that psallere and saltare merely complete poterat. Secure: Identifies the historic infinitive with a reasonable explanation of its effect. Developing: Identifies the words as infinitives without explaining the historic use. Emerging: Little or no accurate grammatical identification.

findings.claim: This is an example of <dfn class="term" data-def="A literary device in which a speaker addresses someone who is absent, dead or otherwise unable to respond, as if they could hear.">apostrophe</dfn>: Camilla speaks directly to a man who can no longer answer.
findings.problem: Mislabelled literary device. Camilla's words over the man she has just speared are a battlefield taunt (a vaunt over a fallen enemy) delivered to someone physically present. The genuine apostrophe in this prescribed passage is the narrator's own address to Camilla at Aeneid 11.664-665 ('quem telo primum, quem postremum, aspera virgo, deicis?'), where Virgil breaks off to speak to his heroine. Offering the wrong example invites students to misapply the term in a style question.
findings.correction: This is a battlefield vaunt — the boast a Homeric warrior makes over a fallen enemy. Virgil also uses apostrophe in this passage, but it is the poet himself who addresses Camilla: quem telo primum, quem postremum, aspera virgo, deicis? — “whom do you strike down first, whom last, fierce maiden?”

findings.claim: Livy blames Tullia specifically for making the new reign’s beginning “a bloody one,” setting up the eventual overthrow of the monarchy.
findings.problem: The phrase in quotation marks is not Livy's. At History 1.48 Livy says Tullia carried her father's blood to her own and her husband's household gods, 'whose anger was the cause that the evil beginning of this reign was, at no long date, followed by a similar end' (malo regni principio). Livy attributes the consequence to the anger of the penates and speaks of an 'evil'/'ill-omened' beginning, not a 'bloody' one, and the quotation should not be presented as his words.
findings.correction: Livy says that Tullia carried her father’s blood to her own and her husband’s household gods, and that their anger meant the evil beginning of the reign was before long followed by a similar end — the overthrow of the monarchy.

findings.claim: In an exam answer, naming this exact detail — whose body, and why the act shocked contemporaries — earns more credit than a general description of “a woman being cruel.”
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how answers are credited. The specification publishes no band descriptors or per-question tariffs for this subject, so no statement about what 'earns more credit' can be supported.
findings.correction: When you write about this source, be specific — say whose body it is and why the act was shocking to a Roman audience — rather than describing it only as “a woman being cruel.”

findings.claim: examiners’ reports repeatedly note that responses which name a device (such as apostrophe or a historic infinitive) without showing how the actual words create that effect are self-limiting
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about examiner behaviour, and 'self-limiting' echoes band-descriptor language. The assessment rules for this qualification publish no band descriptors and say nothing about examiner reports; nothing in the specification supports this claim.
findings.correction: When you are asked to analyse the effect of language, always quote the Latin briefly and give an English gloss straight away: naming a device without showing how the actual words create the effect leaves the analysis incomplete.

findings.claim: Tullia deliberately drove her chariot home over his corpse rather than take a longer route
findings.problem: Livy 1.48 does not mention avoiding a longer route: her driver pulled up in horror at the sight of the body on the road up the Vicus Cyprius, and Tullia, driven by frenzy, ordered him on over it.
findings.correction: when her driver pulled up in horror at the sight of the body lying in the road, Tullia ordered him to drive on straight over her father’s corpse

findings.claim: Source 4: Tullia the Younger’s Chariot
findings.problem: The prescribed material and the resource booklet label the pictures 'Picture 1' to 'Picture 6'; this relief is Picture 4. Using a different label may confuse students looking it up in the booklet they are given in the examination.
findings.correction: Picture 4: Tullia the Younger’s Chariot

findings.claim: {"q": "In the bas relief that is Source 4, whose corpse does Tullia the Younger drive her chariot over?", "a": "Her own father, King Servius Tullius."}
findings.problem: The prescribed picture is labelled 'Picture 4' in the resource booklet, not 'Source 4'.
findings.correction: {"q": "In the bas relief that is Picture 4, whose corpse does Tullia the Younger drive her chariot over?", "a": "Her own father, King Servius Tullius."}

findings.claim: In the Aeneid, the Etruscan king Evander tells Aeneas about the tyrant Mezentius, who ruled the city of Agylla for many years
findings.problem: Evander is not Etruscan. In Aeneid 8 he is the Arcadian (Greek) king of Pallanteum on the site of Rome, Aeneas's host and father of Pallas; the Etruscan king in this passage is Mezentius himself, whom the set-text booklet glosses as 'Mezentius (the Etruscan king)'. A student copying this would misidentify the speaker's nationality and confuse him with the villain he denounces.
findings.correction: In the Aeneid, Aeneas's host Evander, the Arcadian king of Pallanteum, tells Aeneas about the Etruscan tyrant Mezentius, who ruled the city of Agylla for many years

findings.claim: A coin minted by Brutus and Cassius after the assassination of Julius Caesar shows a freedman’s cap between two daggers
findings.problem: The 'Ides of March' (EID MAR) denarius was issued by Marcus Junius Brutus alone, through his moneyer Lucius Plaetorius Cestianus, in 43-42 BC; the obverse carries Brutus's own portrait and the legend BRVT IMP L PLAET CEST. Cassius did not co-issue it - the two daggers are usually explained as standing for the assassins, which is probably what has been misread as joint minting.
findings.correction: A coin minted by Brutus after the assassination of Julius Caesar shows a freedman’s cap between two daggers, one for each of the chief assassins

findings.claim: anti-hero: A morally flawed or repellent character who serves as the villain or negative example in a piece of literature.
findings.problem: This conflates 'anti-hero' with 'villain'. In standard literary usage an anti-hero is a central figure who conspicuously lacks the conventional virtues of a hero (courage, honour, self-control) while still occupying the hero's place in the narrative - which is precisely why Tacitus's Sejanus can be asked about as 'hero or villain?'. Defining the term as simply 'the villain' is a misleading simplification that would weaken an evaluative answer. (Same definition also appears in the data-def of the dfn in content_html and should be changed there too.)
findings.correction: anti-hero: A central figure who lacks the conventional virtues of a hero - courage used well, honour, self-control - and who is presented as a flawed or repellent example rather than a model to admire.

findings.claim: As a young man he attached himself to the family of the emperor Augustus
findings.problem: The set text is more specific: 'cum iuvenis esset divi Augusti nepotem sectatus est' - as a young man he accompanied (was part of the retinue of) the grandson of the divine Augustus, not the imperial family in general. The precise detail is the kind of point a comprehension question could target.
findings.correction: As a young man he attached himself to the retinue of the grandson of the deified Augustus

findings.claim: Source 1 is a coin from the reign of the emperor Lucius Verus.
findings.problem: The prescribed booklet caption for Picture 1 says only "A coin showing Aeneas leaving Troy" — it gives no reign, and no Aeneas-fleeing-Troy coin type is attributed to Lucius Verus. The well-known types showing Aeneas carrying Anchises and leading Ascanius are the Julius Caesar denarius of 47–46 BC and imperial issues under Hadrian (Ilion) and Antoninus Pius (RIC III 615). The attribution is invented and students may repeat it as fact.
findings.correction: Source 1 is a Roman coin showing Aeneas — the legendary ancestor of the Roman people — leaving burning Troy, leading his son Ascanius by the hand while carrying his elderly father, Anchises, on his back.

findings.claim: Anchises himself holds the household gods, the penates, meaning the family’s protective spirits travel with them into exile.
findings.problem: The booklet caption for Picture 1 describes only Aeneas leaving Troy; it does not identify what Anchises holds. On the Caesarian coin type it is Aeneas who carries the Palladium, and descriptions of the imperial types vary. The detail should be hedged as a Virgilian association (Aeneid 2.717) rather than asserted as visible in the source.
findings.correction: In Virgil’s account Anchises carries the sacred objects and household gods, the penates, so the family’s protective spirits travel with them into exile.

findings.claim: {"q": "What does Anchises carry as he escapes Troy in Source 1?", "a": "The household gods, the penates."}
findings.problem: Same issue: the prescribed caption does not state what Anchises holds on the coin, so this cannot be set as a recall fact about the source.
findings.correction: {"q": "In Virgil's account of the escape from Troy, what sacred objects does Anchises carry?", "a": "The household gods, the penates."}

findings.claim: a vague description earns far fewer marks than a precise one
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marking. The specification publishes no per-question tariffs and no band descriptors for this subject, so no statement can be made about how many marks a given style of answer earns.
findings.correction: a vague description does not show the detailed knowledge the question is asking for, while a precise one does

findings.claim: The most common mistake with source questions is describing what a source shows without linking that description to a specific factual point.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about candidate behaviour/exam frequency. Nothing in the specification supports a claim about the most common mistake in source questions.
findings.correction: A weak answer to a source question describes what a source shows without linking that description to a specific factual point.

findings.claim: Source questions reward candidates who name a specific detail in the source and then connect it directly to a fact about the person or event it shows — not a general impression.
findings.problem: Presented as a Key Fact about how answers are rewarded, but the specification publishes no mark schemes or band descriptors for this subject, so no claim can be made about what source questions reward.
findings.correction: A strong source answer names a specific detail in the source and then connects it directly to a fact about the person or event it shows, rather than giving a general impression.

findings.claim: Naming a device alone earns very little credit. You must quote the Latin, give a short translation, and explain the effect it creates.
findings.problem: Invented claim about credit awarded. The specification gives no mark tariffs or band descriptors, so the lesson cannot state what naming a device "earns".
findings.correction: Naming a device on its own does not show analysis. To analyse the effect you need to quote the Latin, give a short translation, and explain the effect it creates.

findings.claim: A full-credit style answer always has three parts: the Latin quotation, an accurate short translation, and a specific explanation of the effect — never the device name on its own.
findings.problem: "Full-credit" is a fabricated mark-scheme claim; the specification publishes no band descriptors or per-question tariffs. The three-part structure is legitimate teaching advice, but it must not be presented as a marking requirement.
findings.correction: A thorough style answer has three parts: the Latin quotation, an accurate short translation, and a specific explanation of the effect — never the device name on its own.

findings.claim: The most common weakness in these answers is relying on only one text.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about how candidates typically perform. The specification says only that the extended evaluative response requires relevant evidence from across the whole theme.
findings.correction: An answer that relies on only one text cannot meet the requirement to use evidence from across the whole theme.

findings.claim: ‘the coin shows two daggers either side of a cap’ is worth more than ‘the coin shows freedom symbols’
findings.problem: A comparative mark-value claim, which the specification cannot support: it publishes no per-question tariffs, mark schemes or band descriptors for this subject.
findings.correction: ‘the coin shows two daggers either side of a cap’ gives the precise evidence your explanation needs, while ‘the coin shows freedom symbols’ does not

findings.claim: The extended evaluative response must draw evidence from across the whole theme, weighing at least three different texts or sources to reach a clear judgement.
findings.problem: The "at least three different texts or sources" threshold is invented. The specification states only that at least one question demands an extended evaluative response containing relevant evidence from across the whole theme; it sets no minimum number of texts or sources.
findings.correction: The extended evaluative response must draw evidence from across the whole theme, ranging beyond a single passage or source to build a sustained line of reasoning and reach a clear judgement.

findings.claim: Read this sentence: 'puer in via ambulabat et amicum vidit.' Answer in English: where was the boy, and what did he do when he saw his friend?
findings.problem: The question asks for something the Latin does not state. 'puer in via ambulabat et amicum vidit' means 'the boy was walking in the street and saw his friend' — there is no action following the seeing. The accompanying mark scheme itself expects only the location and 'the action of seeing the friend', so the question as worded is unanswerable from the Latin and would mislead a student practising precise comprehension.
findings.correction: Read this sentence: 'puer in via ambulabat et amicum vidit.' Answer in English: where was the boy walking, and whom did he see?

findings.claim: Mastering: Produces an accurate, natural translation that correctly renders the perfect passive participle (was captured) and the verb tense of liberavit throughout.
findings.problem: Grammatical mislabel. In 'miles a militibus captus est' the form meaning 'was captured' is the perfect passive indicative (perfect passive participle 'captus' + 'est'); the participle on its own means 'having been captured'. Glossing the participle as 'was captured' teaches students to equate a participle with a finite passive verb.
findings.correction: Mastering: Produces an accurate, natural translation that correctly renders the perfect passive verb captus est ('was captured', participle + est) and the tense of liberavit throughout.

findings.claim: Writing “went” for advenit — he or she arrived loses the mark, even though the general sense of movement is roughly right.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marking behaviour. The stated assessment rules publish no per-question tariffs and no band descriptors, so no statement about a specific answer definitely losing a mark can be supported; the lesson's own practice mark scheme treats 'came' for advenit as still broadly accurate, which contradicts the absolute claim.
findings.correction: Writing “went” for advenit — he or she arrived is not a safe answer, because it does not give the precise meaning of the verb actually written.

findings.claim: This single task carries more of the marks for the language paper than almost any other question, so a reliable method matters here more than anywhere else on the paper.
findings.problem: The specification publishes no per-question mark tariffs and no question counts for the language paper, so a comparison with 'almost any other question' is not supportable. The only figure the specification gives is that the passage translated into English carries 35% of the marks for this component (comprehension on parts one and three totalling 55%).
findings.correction: The translation of the middle passage carries 35% of the marks for the language paper, so a reliable method matters here more than anywhere else on the paper.

findings.claim: Mixing up these two participles is one of the most common ways marks are lost on the language paper.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about candidate performance and examiner behaviour; no published awarding body document quoted in the assessment rules states which errors are most common or where most marks are lost.
findings.correction: Mixing up these two participles changes both the timing and the direction of the action, so the sentence no longer says what the Latin says.

findings.claim: Choosing an approximate English word for a Latin verb — writing 'went' when the Latin says advenit (arrived) — loses the mark even when the general sense of the sentence is right.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how the translation is marked. The specification publishes no mark tariffs, mark schemes or band descriptors for this component, so the lesson cannot assert that a particular slip 'loses the mark'.
findings.correction: Choosing an approximate English word for a Latin verb — writing 'went' when the Latin says advenit (arrived) — changes what the Latin actually says, even when the general sense of the sentence is right.

findings.claim: Use the precise English meaning of each word rather than an approximate one, since an approximate translation loses the mark even if the general sense is right.
findings.problem: Same unevidenced marking claim: the specification publishes no mark schemes or tariffs for the translation question, so the lesson cannot state what does or does not 'lose the mark'.
findings.correction: Use the precise English meaning of each word rather than an approximate one, because an approximate word makes your English say something the Latin does not.

findings.claim: write your literal draft on the page first — it protects your grammar marks even if the final phrasing is clumsy
findings.problem: Invented marking detail: the specification does not describe separate 'grammar marks' within the translation question, and publishes no per-question mark breakdown at all.
findings.correction: write your literal draft on the page first — it helps you check every ending before you commit to the final phrasing, even if that draft reads clumsily

findings.claim: {"q": "Why must 'advenit' be translated as 'arrived', not 'went'?", "a": "Using an approximate word instead of the precise meaning loses the mark."}
findings.problem: The answer rests on an unevidenced claim about marking (the specification publishes no mark schemes or tariffs) and does not actually answer the question, which is about the meaning of the verb.
findings.correction: {"q": "Why must 'advenit' be translated as 'arrived', not 'went'?", "a": "Because advenio specifically means to arrive or reach a place; 'went' is a different verb of motion."}

findings.claim: Polished translation: 'The master praised the slave violently.'
findings.problem: With a verb of praising, vehementer means 'strongly, vigorously, enthusiastically'; 'praised violently' is not idiomatic English and misrepresents the sense the adverb carries here, in a lesson that is itself insisting on precise word choice.
findings.correction: Polished translation: 'The master praised the slave enthusiastically.'

findings.claim: every word needed comes from a dedicated list of one hundred and one English-to-Latin vocabulary items
findings.problem: Fabricated figure. The assessment rules state only that in the translation question "all the English words are taken from the dedicated English-Latin list" — no count is published. The board's own guide-for-teaching states the dedicated vocabulary list for this question comprises 100 words, not 101, so the number is both invented and wrong.
findings.correction: every word needed comes from a dedicated English-to-Latin vocabulary list, which you are expected to learn.

findings.claim: adjectives appear only in the positive or superlative form, never the comparative
findings.problem: Invented restriction. The specification says nothing about which degrees of adjective may appear in the grammar-analysis option; it does state that learners are expected to know "the comparative and superlative forms of every listed adjective". Telling students the comparative can never appear is unsupported and could leave a real form unprepared.
findings.correction: Nouns and adjectives can come from the first three declensions; the specification does not restrict which degrees of adjective may appear, so revise positive, comparative and superlative forms.

findings.claim: Every case can appear in the passage, but questions only ever ask about the nominative and the accusative.
findings.problem: Invented claim about question content. The specification publishes no restriction on which cases may be questioned in the grammar option; it says only that the question covers "the recognition, analysis and explanation of syntax and accidence within a short passage of Latin". Students revising only two cases would be under-prepared.
findings.correction: Any case may appear in the passage, and you may be asked to recognise and explain forms in any of them, so revise the full range of case endings.

findings.claim: The pronouns hic and ille, and clauses introduced by quod (‘because’) or ubi (‘when’), may appear in the passage but will never themselves be the subject of a question.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about what examiners will and will not ask. The specification states no such exclusion for demonstratives or for quod/ubi clauses in the grammar-analysis question.
findings.correction: Demonstratives such as hic and ille, and clauses introduced by quod ('because') or ubi ('when'), may appear in the passage, so be ready to recognise and explain them.

findings.claim: Which forms of adjective are allowed in the short final section's grammar-analysis option? — correct answer: 'Positive and superlative only'
findings.problem: The question tests an invented rule. The specification sets no such limit on adjective degree in the grammar-analysis question, and it expects knowledge of comparatives and superlatives of every listed adjective.
findings.correction: Replace with: 'In the short final section's grammar-analysis option, which noun declensions may appear?' — options: 'First declension only' / 'First and second only' / 'The first three declensions' / 'All five declensions'; correct answer: 'The first three declensions'.

findings.claim: {"q": "In the grammar-analysis option, which adjective forms are allowed?", "a": "Positive and superlative forms, never comparative."}
findings.problem: Repeats the invented restriction on adjective degree; the specification publishes no such rule and does require knowledge of comparative forms.
findings.correction: {"q": "In the grammar-analysis option, which declensions can the nouns and adjectives come from?", "a": "The first three declensions."}

findings.claim: {"q": "In the grammar-analysis option, which two cases are actually tested?", "a": "Nominative and accusative only."}
findings.problem: Repeats the invented claim that only two cases are questioned. The specification does not limit the cases that may be recognised, analysed or explained.
findings.correction: {"q": "In the grammar-analysis option, which cases may you be asked about?", "a": "Any case that appears in the passage."}

findings.claim: Translate this simple Latin sentence into English, using only the vocabulary and endings allowed in the short final section: puellae dominos laudant.
findings.problem: Misattributes the task. The short final section offers only translation from English into Latin or grammar recognition and explanation; translation into English belongs to the middle part of the three-part narrative. The framing implies a Latin-to-English translation appears in the final section.
findings.correction: Translate this simple Latin sentence into English: puellae dominos laudant. (Practice of this kind supports the translation part of the three-part narrative.)

findings.claim: the language paper checks knowledge of <dfn class="term" data-def="An English word that has developed from a Latin word and still shares part of its meaning.">derivation</dfn> links between Latin and English throughout its questions
findings.problem: The specification states only that the language component assesses knowledge of derivation links between Latin and English; it does not say derivation is tested 'throughout its questions'.
findings.correction: the language paper also assesses knowledge of <dfn class="term" data-def="An English word that has developed from a Latin word and still shares part of its meaning.">derivation</dfn> links between Latin and English

findings.claim: Livy prefers the second, more widely believed version: enormous rafts, one measuring 200 feet by 50 feet, were covered with earth so the elephants would think they were walking on solid ground, then floated and towed across while attached to smaller rafts.
findings.problem: The procedure is described the wrong way round. In Passage D (Livy 21.28) the large raft (200 feet by 50 feet) was tethered to the bank by strong cables so it would not drift, and served as an earth-covered pier; a second raft, equally wide but only 100 feet long, was attached to it, the elephants were driven onto that one, and it was then detached and dragged across by light craft. The big raft never crossed the river. A question on the method would penalise the version given here.
findings.correction: Livy prefers the second, more widely believed version: a raft 200 feet long and 50 feet wide was moored to the bank by strong cables and covered with earth like a bridge, so the elephants would think they were walking on solid ground; a second raft, equally wide but 100 feet long, was attached to it, and once the elephants had been driven onto it (led by the females) it was detached and towed across the river by light craft, and the operation was repeated.

findings.claim: naming a device such as alliteration or hyperbaton without explaining its effect earns very little
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about how answers are marked. The assessment rules quoted from the specification publish no per-question tariffs and no band descriptors, and say nothing about how much credit device-spotting attracts, so this claim cannot be supported.
findings.correction: naming a device such as alliteration or hyperbaton is only the starting point — you must go on to explain what it does to the reader

findings.claim: By the end of Passage E, the Carthaginian army has not yet begun the climb itself
findings.problem: Passage E ends with the army already ascending: erigentibus in primos agmen clivos ('to the men leading the column up to the first slopes'), with the mountain tribesmen appearing above them. The lesson's own earlier sentence says the column 'starts climbing the first slopes', so the two statements conflict.
findings.correction: By the end of Passage E the Carthaginian army has only begun to climb the first slopes — the worst of the ascent, and the descent that follows, belongs to the next stage of the story.

findings.claim: By the end of Passage E the army has only reached the foothills of the Alps
findings.problem: Passage E has the column already moving up the first slopes (erigentibus in primos agmen clivos) when the montani appear on the heights, so 'only reached the foothills' understates where the narrative has got to.
findings.correction: By the end of Passage E the army has begun to climb the first slopes of the Alps, and Livy has already used oxymoron and hyperbaton to build dread before the worst of the ascent.

findings.claim: After the killing, Evander says the Ara Maxima was founded in Cacus’s honour, with Potitius as its first priest and the house of Pinarii as its guardians.
findings.problem: The altar is founded in honour of HERCULES, not Cacus. The prescribed booklet (Section G) reads: "Potitius the first founder with the house of Pinarii as guardians of the sacred rites of Hercules, set up in the grove this altar which is always called by us the Greatest Altar" (Latin H: 'primusque Potitius', 'Herculei custos Pinaria sacri'). Cacus is the monster killed at the altar's mythical site; the cult at the Ara Maxima in the Forum Boarium is Hercules' cult. Teaching that the Ara Maxima honoured Cacus inverts the whole aetiology the narrative exists to explain.
findings.correction: After the killing, Evander says the Ara Maxima was founded in Hercules’s honour, with Potitius as its first founder and priest and the house of Pinarii as guardians of Hercules’s sacred rites.

findings.claim: reading them as active or present-tense loses marks in comprehension and analysis questions
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about mark loss / examiner behaviour. The assessment rules publish no per-question tariffs, no band descriptors and say nothing about marks being lost for particular grammatical misreadings, so this cannot be substantiated.
findings.correction: reading them as active or present-tense changes the meaning of the sentence, so it is worth checking the ending and voice before you translate or comment on them

findings.claim: naming a device without any supporting quotation earns very little credit
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about how responses are credited. The specification quoted in the assessment rules publishes no band descriptors or per-question mark guidance, so no claim about what does or does not earn credit can be made.
findings.correction: naming a device on its own does not show its effect, so always anchor the point in the Latin phrase and its English meaning before you explain what it achieves

findings.claim: Match each term to its correct description. Left: ["Verna", "Vilicus", "Servi publici"]; Right: ["A status of legal disgrace attached to certain performers", "A child born into slavery to an enslaved mother", "The overseer who managed enslaved workers on a farm"], order [1, 2, 0]
findings.problem: The mapping pairs 'Servi publici' with 'A status of legal disgrace attached to certain performers', which is the definition of infamia, not of servi publici. The source booklet (Slavery in the Roman World, 'Servi publici') defines servi publici as enslaved people owned by a community, under the authority of the Roman Senate or a local council. A student memorising this card would give a wrong definition.
findings.correction: Right options should be: ["Enslaved people owned by the Roman state or a local community", "A child born into slavery to an enslaved mother", "The overseer who managed enslaved workers on a farm"], with order [1, 2, 0].

findings.claim: Livy notes that when Scipio freed skilled workers at New Carthage, he made them public slaves “with the not distant hope of freedom if they should actively exert themselves in providing the equipment for war”.
findings.problem: Inverts the source. Livy, ab urbe condita XXVI.47.1-2 (in the resource booklet, and confirmed on Perseus) says Scipio released the free citizens of New Carthage, but the roughly two thousand captured artisans were declared public slaves of the Roman people — they were enslaved, not freed, and were only promised the prospect of freedom later if they worked hard on war equipment.
findings.correction: Livy notes that at New Carthage Scipio declared the roughly two thousand captured artisans to be public slaves of the Roman people, “with the not distant hope of freedom if they should actively exert themselves in providing the equipment for war”.

findings.claim: a vague description of a picture or a general statement will not gain full credit on its own
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how marks are awarded. The specification publishes no band descriptors, no per-question tariffs and no statement about what does or does not earn full credit, so this marking claim is not supported by any published document.
findings.correction: When a question asks you to explain a feature of Roman civilisation, name a specific fact or source and say exactly what it shows, rather than describing a picture or making a general statement.

findings.claim: Cicero wrote anxiously to a friend about his sick secretary Tiro, begging for news of his recovery
findings.problem: The prescribed source (Cicero, Letters IV = Fam. XVI.10, in the Component 3B resource booklet) is a letter written directly TO Tiro, not to a third party about him: 'I of course wish you to come to me, but I dread the journey for you… be sure, my dear Tiro, that I find you there strong and well.' The addressee is a checkable detail a student could be asked about in source work.
findings.correction: Cicero wrote anxiously to his sick secretary Tiro himself, telling him not to risk the journey until he was fully recovered and saying that without him his studies were at a standstill

findings.claim: In 73 BC the rebels defeated the armies of both consuls and the governor of Cisalpine Gaul, then marched the length of Italy plundering as they went.
findings.problem: The resource booklet dates only the first Roman forces sent against the rebels to 73 BC; the defeat of both consuls and of the governor of Cisalpine Gaul belongs to 72 BC, which is why the booklet says Crassus, praetor of 73 BC, was given imperium 'after the defeat of the consuls' in 72 BC. Dating the consular defeats to 73 BC contradicts the booklet's own chronology and standard accounts (Plutarch, Crassus 9; Appian, Civil Wars 1.14).
findings.correction: In 73 BC the rebels easily beat the first Roman forces sent against them, and in 72 BC they defeated the armies of both consuls and the governor of Cisalpine Gaul, marching the length of Italy plundering as they went.

findings.claim: He then built a wall across an isthmus to trap Spartacus’s army, forcing a final battle.
findings.problem: In the booklet's Plutarch narrative (Life of Crassus 10-11) Spartacus was not held by the wall: he filled part of the ditch with earth, timber and branches and sent a third of his force across, escaping the trap. The final battle came later, after his men refused to avoid engagement.
findings.correction: He then built a wall and ditch across the isthmus at Rhegium to pen Spartacus in, but Spartacus filled part of the ditch and broke out with part of his force; the decisive battle came later, when his overconfident followers forced an engagement in Lucania.

findings.claim: In practice, few enslaved people had the resources to do this quickly, so most who gained freedom this way had built up their savings over many years of trusted service.
findings.problem: The set booklet states only that "It is unlikely that many had the means to do so" — i.e. buying freedom was rare in itself, not merely slow; and Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities 4.24.4-8) says only "a few slaves" paid a ransom fee. The claim about "many years of trusted service" is not supported by any source in the booklet.
findings.correction: In practice it is unlikely that many enslaved people ever had the means to buy their freedom, and ancient writers suggest that only a few did so, paying a ransom fee out of their savings.

findings.claim: Each method gave the same basic legal freedom, but only some counted as full, formal manumission recognised by the state.
findings.problem: Overstates the equivalence of the routes. The booklet distinguishes formal manumission (manumissio iusta, before a magistrate) from informal freeing before the owner's friends, and includes Pliny, Letters 7.16, headed "Informal manumission could be formalised at a later date" — showing that an informal declaration did not give the same legal position until it was formalised.
findings.correction: Formal manumission before a magistrate was recognised by the state, while an informal declaration in front of the owner’s friends left a person free in practice but needed to be formalised later to give the full legal position.

findings.claim: This lesson looks at three examples named in the specification: the Lupercalia, a February rite of purification; Bona Dea, a secret women’s festival; and Saturnalia, Rome’s midwinter celebration of gifts and role reversal.
findings.problem: The stated assessment rules prescribe the topic "Roman Festivals and Worship" with five guided areas of study and expressly state that NO specific ancient source materials are prescribed; individual festivals such as Lupercalia, Bona Dea and Saturnalia are not named as prescribed content anywhere in the specification. Claiming they are "named in the specification" is an invented exam claim (the resource booklet is only a teaching-support publication, not a definitive catalogue).
findings.correction: This lesson looks at three major Roman festivals: the Lupercalia, a February rite of purification; Bona Dea, a secret women's festival; and Saturnalia, Rome's midwinter celebration of gifts and role reversal.

findings.claim: her real name was considered too sacred to say aloud, so this title was used instead
findings.problem: Contradicts the primary source booklet, which states: "'Bona Dea' means 'The Good Goddess'. It is a title given to her, because her name is uncertain." Standard reference works (Oxford Classical Dictionary, s.v. Bona Dea) likewise say the Good Goddess is her title, not her name, and that her name is unknown/uncertain — not that it was unspeakable.
findings.correction: "Bona Dea" is a title rather than a name: her real name is uncertain, so this title was used instead

findings.claim: During Saturnalia, enslaved members of a household became masters for the duration of the festival and were waited on by their owners
findings.problem: The source booklet says "Enslaved members of the household became masters for a day and were waited on by their masters" — the reversal was a single day, not the whole 17-23 December period. The lesson also contradicts itself, writing elsewhere "For the length of the festival, enslaved members of a household became masters for a day".
findings.correction: During Saturnalia, enslaved members of a household became masters for a day and were waited on by their owners

findings.claim: For the length of the festival, enslaved members of a household became masters for a day: they were waited on by their own owners
findings.problem: Internally contradictory and unsupported by the source booklet, which limits the reversal to one day ("became masters for a day").
findings.correction: For one day of the festival, enslaved members of a household became masters: they were waited on by their own owners

findings.claim: {"q": "According to Ovid, why was a goat sacrificed at the Lupercalia?", "a": "Because the goat was sacred to the god Faunus."}
findings.problem: Misstates Ovid's explanation as given in the source booklet: Ovid links both the nakedness of the Luperci and the goat sacrifice to Faunus's humiliation when clothing deceived him during his attempt on Omphale ("Since clothes fooled him, the god hates deceptive clothing"). Being sacred to Faunus is not the reason Ovid gives.
findings.correction: {"q": "According to Ovid, why was a goat sacrificed at the Lupercalia?", "a": "Because a swap of clothes humiliated Faunus when he pursued Omphale, so his rites recall that goat-skin deception."}

findings.claim: Bona Dea: 'The Good Goddess' — an Italian goddess worshipped only by women, with rites held twice a year and men strictly excluded.
findings.problem: Overstated: the booklet (and Oxford Classical Dictionary) record that men were rigorously excluded from the nocturnal December ceremony, not that the goddess was worshipped only by women; the booklet's own Ovid extract notes exceptions ("except any (men) she commands to come"), and she also had a public temple on the Aventine.
findings.correction: Bona Dea: 'The Good Goddess' — a title given to an Italian goddess whose name is uncertain; she had rites twice a year, and men were rigorously excluded from her nocturnal December ceremony.

findings.claim: He then offers a second: that the ceremonies imitate Romulus and Remus running joyfully back to the spot where the she-wolf had nursed them, after defeating the tyrant Amulius
findings.problem: In the source booklet Plutarch attributes this explanation to another writer ("a certain poet … says that Romulus and Remus, after the conquest of Amulius, ran joyfully to the place where the wolf suckled them"), rather than advancing it as his own.
findings.correction: He then reports a second, which he credits to a poet: that the ceremonies imitate Romulus and Remus running joyfully back to the spot where the she-wolf had nursed them, after defeating the tyrant Amulius

findings.claim: Vague answers that do not say exactly what a source shows lose marks.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about marking/examiner behaviour. The stated assessment rules publish no band descriptors, no per-question tariffs and no statement that marks are deducted for vagueness; the specification only states that at least one question demands an extended evaluative response using material from across the chosen topic. Claims about how marks are lost must not be invented.
findings.correction: Answers are stronger when they say exactly what a named source or ritual detail shows, rather than describing Roman religion in general terms.

findings.claim: Pliny the Elder records that its bronze capitals and Caryatid columns were considered masterpieces of design.
findings.problem: Misreports the source (Pliny, Natural History 34.7, as given in the resource booklet). Pliny says the capitals placed by Agrippa were made of Syracusan bronze; it is the Caryatides made by Diogenes of Athens, together with the statues on the roof, that are described as masterpieces of excellence — the capitals are not called masterpieces.
findings.correction: Pliny the Elder records that its capitals were made of Syracusan bronze, and that the Caryatid columns made by Diogenes of Athens, along with the statues on the roof, were considered masterpieces.

findings.claim: The father and grandfather were dutiful, but the son who inherits the house neglects his offerings — so the Lar treats him just as carelessly in return.
findings.problem: Contradicts the set booklet's extract of Plautus, Pot of Gold, lines 1-30 (the prologue of the Aulularia). There it is the grandfather alone who is dutiful (he entrusts the buried money to the Lar); of the next generation the Lar says 'I began to take notice of how the son would treat me, whether he would be more or less dutiful than his father. He was far less dutiful, as it turned out, and far less respectful to me. Likewise, I did as little as possible for him.' The lesson wrongly makes the father dutiful as well.
findings.correction: It was the grandfather who dutifully entrusted the buried money to the Lar; his son was 'far less dutiful' and 'far less respectful', so the Lar in turn 'did as little as possible for him', and the present owner is of much the same character.

findings.claim: alongside the toga praetexta — the striped toga that marked out free-born childhood
findings.problem: Mistaken gloss of the Latin term. The toga praetexta (praetexta = 'bordered') was a white toga with a broad purple border, worn by free-born children (and by certain magistrates and priests) — it was not striped (Britannica, 'toga praetexta'; Dickinson College Commentaries on the purple-bordered toga of Roman boys and girls).
findings.correction: alongside the toga praetexta — the purple-bordered toga that marked out free-born childhood

findings.claim: Romans held three annual festivals connected to the dead: the Parentalia (13th–21st February), its final public day the Feralia, and the Lemuria (9th, 11th and 13th May).
findings.problem: The Feralia is not a separate annual festival: the booklet treats the festivals of the dead as the Parentalia and the Lemuria, with the Feralia as the public ceremony held on the last day of the Parentalia ('On the last day a public ceremony, the Feralia, was held'). The attached revision tip ('name the three Roman festivals of the dead, with the month each was held in') compounds this by implying the Feralia had its own date and month.
findings.correction: Romans held two annual festivals connected to the dead: the Parentalia (13th–21st February), whose final day was the public ceremony of the Feralia, and the Lemuria (9th, 11th and 13th May). [Revision tip: "Cover this and name the two Roman festivals of the dead, with the month each was held in and what happened on the Feralia."]

findings.claim: The fercula — main course — is a young kid
findings.problem: Wrong number: fercula is the nominative/accusative PLURAL of ferculum (2nd declension neuter, 'course/dish'), as the resource booklet's own vocabulary note confirms ('ferculum ferculi n. - main course (in a meal)'). The lesson presents the plural form as the singular term and glosses it as a singular, and then treats it as a singular subject ('is a young kid'). A student copying this will write an ungrammatical form.
findings.correction: The ferculum (plural fercula) — main course — is a young kid

findings.claim: {"term": "fercula", "definition": "The main course of a Roman dinner, served after the starter and before the dessert."}
findings.problem: The headword is a plural form defined as a singular. The booklet glosses the singular as 'ferculum ferculi n. - main course (in a meal)'; fercula is nominative/accusative plural (Juvenal's 'fercula nunc audi' = 'hear now the main courses').
findings.correction: {"term": "ferculum (plural fercula)", "definition": "A main course or dish of a Roman dinner, carried in to the diners; the plural fercula is used by Juvenal for the courses of his meal."}

findings.claim: {"q": "What is the Latin term for the main course of a Roman dinner?", "a": "Fercula."}
findings.problem: Gives the plural form as the answer to a question asking for the (singular) term. The booklet's vocabulary list gives 'ferculum ferculi n. - main course'; fercula is the plural, as used in Juvenal line 1.
findings.correction: {"q": "What is the Latin term for the main course of a Roman dinner?", "a": "Ferculum (plural fercula)."}

findings.claim: dormice sprinkled with honey and poppy seed — balanced on little bronze bridges
findings.problem: The set text does not say the bridges were bronze: 'ponticuli etiam ferruminati sustinebant glires melle ac papavere sparsos' — 'little bridges soldered (to the plate) were holding up dormice sprinkled with honey and poppy seeds'. The only bronze object in the passage is the Corinthian-bronze donkey (asellus Corinthius); the dishes in this part of the scene are silver (nomen Trimalchionis inscriptum erat et argenti pondus). 'Bronze' is an invented detail.
findings.correction: dormice sprinkled with honey and poppy seed — held up on little soldered bridges (ponticuli ferruminati) attached to the dish

findings.claim: always quote the Latin words themselves (with a brief translation) rather than only naming a device — writing “alliteration” on its own earns very little credit
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how answers are credited. The stated assessment rules publish no per-question tariffs and no band descriptors, so no claim about how much credit a bare technique-label 'earns' can be supported. The pedagogical advice itself is sound; the credit claim must go.
findings.correction: always quote the Latin words themselves (with a brief translation) and explain their effect, rather than only naming a device — naming “alliteration” without showing what it does in the line leaves your point unsupported

findings.claim: his <dfn class="term" data-def="A wealthy or powerful Roman who supported clients, who in return owed him loyalty and services.">patron</dfn> still serves him worse food than everyone else
findings.problem: In Epigrams 3.60 the contrast is consistently between the poet (mihi) and his host (tibi) alone — 'cur mihi non eadem, quae tibi, cena datur?'. The poem says nothing about other guests being better fed than Martial; the graded treatment of different ranks of guest belongs to Pliny's letter, not this epigram.
findings.correction: his <dfn class="term" data-def="A wealthy or powerful Roman who supported clients, who in return owed him loyalty and services.">patron</dfn> still serves him worse food than the host eats himself

findings.claim: Homegrown produce was not restricted at all, because it did not cost money and did not display wealth in the same way.
findings.problem: Gellius' text exempts 'quidquid esset natum e terra, vite, arbore' — whatever was produced from the earth, a vine or a tree — without any reference to it being homegrown or to the reason for the exemption. 'Homegrown' and the stated motive are the lesson's inference, not what the source says.
findings.correction: Produce of the earth, the vine and the tree was not restricted at all, while meat and pickled fish — the goods that had to be bought — were capped by weight. Many scholars link this to the idea that bought foods were the visible markers of extravagance.

findings.claim: This theme studies four Latin texts about hospitality: Ovid’s story of Baucis and Philemon (good hospitality), Ovid’s story of Lycaon (hospitality refused a god), and a letter and an epigram by Pliny and Martial (how not to treat your guests).
findings.problem: The prescribed material for this theme contains eight Latin texts, not four: Aulus Gellius Attic Nights 2.24, Juvenal Satire 11.64-80, Martial Epigrams 3.60, Ovid Metamorphoses 1.221-239 and 8.664-688, Petronius Cena Trimalchionis 31-34 (adapted), Pliny Letters 2.6 and Seneca de Clementia 1.18. Telling students the theme consists of only four texts (and the accompanying revision tip 'name the four texts studied for this theme') would leave half the assessed prescription unrevised, and the extended evaluative question draws on material from across the whole theme.
findings.correction: This lesson looks at the four prescribed texts that deal most directly with hospitality: Ovid’s story of Baucis and Philemon (good hospitality), Ovid’s story of Lycaon (hospitality refused a god), Pliny’s letter and Martial’s epigram (how not to treat your guests). Remember that the theme as a whole also prescribes Aulus Gellius, Juvenal, Petronius and Seneca, which you must know for the extended evaluative answer. (Revision tip: cover this and name the four hospitality texts covered here, plus the other four texts prescribed for the theme.)

findings.claim: Turned away by household after household, he finally reaches the palace of Lycaon, the cruel king of Arcadia.
findings.problem: This detail belongs to the Baucis and Philemon episode (Metamorphoses 8, where a thousand houses bar their doors), not to the Lycaon episode. In Metamorphoses 1.218-221 Jupiter enters the Arcadian tyrant’s halls, gives signs of his divinity and the crowd begins to pray, while Lycaon mocks their piety (inridet primo pia vota Lycaon). Nothing in the set text or the surrounding narrative says he was refused by household after household.
findings.correction: Jupiter comes to the halls of Lycaon, the cruel king of Arcadia. He gives signs that a god has arrived, and while the ordinary people begin to pray, Lycaon mocks their piety and decides to test the visitor in the worst possible way.

findings.claim: Pliny's host — Divided food and wine into three grades by guest's status
findings.problem: Pliny Letters 2.6 says the wine was divided into three categories (in tria genera ... aliud sibi et nobis, aliud minoribus amicis, aliud suis nostrisque libertis), but the food is described in two tiers only: sumptuous dishes for himself and a few (sibi et paucis opima quaedam) and cheap, tiny portions for the rest (ceteris vilia et minuta). 'Food and wine into three grades' is not supported by the set text.
findings.correction: Pliny's host — Graded his wine into three categories and served cheap food to all but himself and a favoured few

findings.claim: Mastering: Explains the three grades of wine and food accurately and gives a clear reason for Pliny's disapproval (equal treatment of all guests).
findings.problem: Same error as the matching task: Pliny Letters 2.6 gives three grades of wine only; the food is described in two tiers (opima quaedam for the host and a few, vilia et minuta for the rest). A mark scheme rewarding 'three grades of ... food' would credit an inaccurate answer.
findings.correction: Mastering: Explains accurately that the wine was divided into three grades (host and chief guests, lesser friends, freedmen) and that better food was reserved for the host and a few others, and gives a clear reason for Pliny's disapproval (equal treatment of all guests).

findings.claim: Mastering: Quotes the Latin accurately with translation and explains in detail how the double negative and word choice emphasise generosity despite poverty.
findings.problem: In 'nec iners pauperque voluntas' there is a single negative (nec), which negates both adjectives iners and pauper. The figure is litotes (understatement by negation), not a double negative; labelling it a double negative teaches students an incorrect grammatical/stylistic term they will reproduce.
findings.correction: Mastering: Quotes the Latin accurately with translation and explains in detail how the litotes (nec negating both iners and pauper) and the word choice emphasise generosity despite poverty.

findings.claim: {"q": "How did Lycaon try to kill his sleeping guest?", "a": "He planned to kill him at night while he slept."}
findings.problem: The answer simply restates the question: the question already supplies 'kill' and 'sleeping', so the card tests nothing.
findings.correction: {"q": "How did Lycaon first plan to attack his divine guest?", "a": "By murdering him unexpectedly at night with a sudden death while he lay in deep sleep."}

findings.claim: {"q": "What does Martial mean by 'cur sine te ceno, cum tecum cenem'?", "a": "Unequal food makes shared dining feel like dining alone."}
findings.problem: The Latin is not verbatim from the set text: the resource booklet reads 'cur sine te ceno, cum tecum, Pontice, cenem?' (Epigrams 3.60.9). The vocative Pontice has been dropped without any mark of omission, so a student copying the card would misquote the line.
findings.correction: {"q": "What does Martial mean by 'cur sine te ceno, cum tecum, Pontice, cenem?'", "a": "Unequal food makes shared dining feel like dining alone."}

findings.claim: Their hospes receive full attention even though the food is plain.
findings.problem: hospes is nominative singular but is used here as the plural subject of 'receive'; the plural is hospites (as in the set text's dis hospitibus). A student copying this will use the wrong form.
findings.correction: Their hospites (guests) receive full attention even though the food is plain.

findings.claim: Once Jupiter and Mercury reveal a hint of who they really are, the couple notice something strange happening at their table.
findings.problem: The order of events in the set text is the reverse: the couple see the mixing bowl refilling itself and the wine growing of its own accord (interea totiens haustum cratera repleri sponte sua per seque vident succrescere vina), and it is this miracle that first shows them their guests are divine — they are astonished at the strangeness (attoniti novitate pavent). The gods make no prior revelation.
findings.correction: The couple notice something strange happening at their table, and it is this that first hints at who their guests really are.

findings.claim: Juvenal’s alliteration in crudi posuere pericula suci — “the raw juice has set aside its dangers”
findings.problem: Mistranslation. In the set text (Juvenal, Satire 11.76-77 as printed in the prescribed booklet: 'nec metuenda tibi, siccatum frigore postquam / autumnum et crudi posuere pericula suci') 'crudi ... suci' is genitive singular dependent on 'pericula', and the subject of 'posuere' is the apples (mala). The booklet's own English gives '[the apples] have set aside autumn, dried up by the cold and [set aside] the dangers of unripe juice.' The lesson's gloss wrongly makes 'crudi suci' the nominative subject, so a student would learn a false case and a false sense.
findings.correction: Juvenal’s alliteration in crudi posuere pericula suci — “[the apples] have laid aside the dangers of raw juice” — uses the repeated p- sound to slow the line down, matching the idea of fruit carefully stored and softened over time.

findings.claim: A fresco possibly showing a politician in a whitened toga distributing bread to the crowd, hinting at the political use of food as a gift.
findings.problem: The 'whitened toga' (toga candida) detail is not supported by the prescribed booklet, which describes Picture 6 only as 'A politician distributes bread to townsfolk, Pompeii, c.AD 79.' Published discussion of this Pompeian bread-distribution fresco notes the main figure's identity (baker or politician) is debated and describes him simply as toga-clad; no source supports 'whitened'.
findings.correction: A fresco showing a politician distributing bread to the townsfolk of Pompeii, hinting at the political use of food as a gift.

findings.claim: {"q": "What does the bread-distribution fresco possibly show a politician doing?", "a": "Distributing bread to the crowd while wearing a whitened toga."}
findings.problem: Same unsupported detail: the prescribed booklet's caption for Picture 6 says only that a politician distributes bread to townsfolk at Pompeii; it says nothing about a whitened toga.
findings.correction: {"q": "What does the prescribed bread-distribution fresco from Pompeii show?", "a": "A politician distributing bread to the townsfolk."}

findings.claim: {"q": "In Martial's poem, what drink does the host enjoy while the guest gets a mussel?", "a": "Oysters fattened in the Lucrine lake."}
findings.problem: The question is factually wrong: oysters are shellfish, not a drink. Martial 3.60.3-4 in the booklet ('ostrea tu sumis stagno saturata Lucrino, / sugitur inciso mitulus ore mihi') contrasts the host's oysters with the guest's mussel, both foods; no drink is mentioned in these lines.
findings.correction: {"q": "In Martial's poem, what shellfish delicacy does the host eat while the guest gets only a mussel?", "a": "Oysters fattened in the Lucrine lake."}

findings.claim: Naming <dfn class="term" data-def="A figure of speech that reverses the order of corresponding words in two paired phrases, for balance or contrast.">chiasmus</dfn> without saying what it does for that particular line earns very little.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how marks are awarded. The stated assessment rules publish no per-question tariffs and no band descriptors, and say nothing about what a bare device-name 'earns'.
findings.correction: Naming <dfn class="term" data-def="A figure of speech that reverses the order of corresponding words in two paired phrases, for balance or contrast.">chiasmus</dfn> is only the starting point: you also need to say what it does for that particular line.

findings.claim: a device named without an explained effect is a self-limiting answer
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about marking behaviour; nothing in the stated assessment rules describes answers as 'self-limiting' or sets out how such answers are credited.
findings.correction: a device named without an explained effect leaves the analysis incomplete, so always add the effect

findings.claim: A common mistake is describing a source in detail without connecting it to a specific factual point about the theme.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about how candidates typically perform; no published document in the stated assessment rules supports a frequency claim about candidate errors.
findings.correction: Take care not to describe a source in detail without connecting it to a specific factual point about the theme.

findings.claim: The garum jar carries its own inscribed label: G(ari) F(los) SCOM(bri) SCAURI EX OFFI(ci)NA SCAURI
findings.problem: Imprecise description of the picture source. The booklet describes Picture 3 as 'Garum, picture from the villa of Aulus Umbricius Scaurus, Pompeii'; the image is the painted/mosaic depiction of a garum urceus with its label from Scaurus's house, not a surviving physical jar. (Scaurus as Pompeii's leading fish-sauce maker and the Mediterranean-wide distribution of his labelled urcei are correct.)
findings.correction: The depicted garum vessel carries its own label: G(ari) F(los) SCOM(bri) SCAURI EX OFFI(ci)NA SCAURI

findings.claim: Luckily for Hannibal, the tribesmen showed themselves too early and lost their chance to inflict real damage.
findings.problem: The prescribed text does not say the tribesmen revealed themselves prematurely. Passage E reads 'qui, si valles occultiores insedissent, coorti ad pugnam repente ingentem fugam stragemque dedissent' — 'who, if they had taken possession of the more hidden valleys and suddenly leapt out to battle, would have inflicted huge flight and slaughter'. Livy's point is that they posted themselves on visible heights instead of concealed valleys, so their position, not their timing, cost them the surprise.
findings.correction: Luckily for Hannibal, the tribesmen had posted themselves in full view on the heights: Livy notes that had they hidden in the more concealed valleys and rushed out suddenly, they would have inflicted huge slaughter and panic.

findings.claim: {"q": "Why did the mountain tribesmen's ambush in Passage E fail to do much damage?", "a": "They showed themselves too early, losing the advantage of surprise."}
findings.problem: Contradicts the source text: Livy writes that they would have caused huge slaughter 'si valles occultiores insedissent' — if they had occupied the more hidden valleys. The weakness was that they were visible on the heights, not that they appeared too early.
findings.correction: {"q": "Why, according to Livy, did the mountain tribesmen fail to inflict slaughter on the column in Passage E?", "a": "They sat in plain view on the heights instead of hiding in the more concealed valleys."}

findings.claim: Passage G survives only in English within the prescribed narrative
findings.problem: Misleading: Livy's Latin for this section (History 21.36) survives; it is simply supplied in English translation in the prescribed narrative, which pairs continuous Latin with adjacent passages in English that extend the storyline.
findings.correction: Passage G is one of the sections supplied in English translation within the prescribed narrative, but it describes the single most dangerous moment of the crossing.

findings.claim: Hannibal has already slipped past the Roman fleet at the mouth of the Rhone and marched east with help from friendly Gallic tribes
findings.problem: Neither detail is supported by the prescribed narrative. The linking summary says only that Cornelius Scipio had sailed with an army to Massilia, unaware until arrival that Hannibal had begun to cross the Rhône; and Passage E says Hannibal reached the Alps 'cum bona pace incolarum ea loca Gallorum' — with the peaceful acquiescence of the local Gauls, not their active help.
findings.correction: By Passage E of Livy's narrative, Hannibal has crossed the Rhône — with Scipio only learning of it after landing at Massilia — and has marched on towards the Alps, mostly over open country and unopposed by the local Gallic peoples.

findings.claim: A response that only quotes and translates, without saying why the choice is effective, is self-limiting — so is a response that lists every device in a passage without picking out the best example. In comprehension answers, be precise: a verb meaning ‘arrived’ is not the same as ‘went’, and small differences like this can cost a mark.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertions about marking behaviour ('self-limiting', 'can cost a mark'). The stated assessment rules publish no per-question tariffs and no band descriptors, so no claim can be made about what marking penalises.
findings.correction: For any Literary Style question, follow three steps: name the device, quote a short piece of Latin exactly as printed in the text, and explain what effect it has on the reader. A quotation with a translation but no comment on effect leaves the analysis incomplete, and picking one strong example is more useful than listing every device. In comprehension answers, be precise about meaning: a verb meaning 'arrived' is not the same as 'went'.

findings.claim: quote a short piece of Latin exactly as printed in the resource booklet
findings.problem: The stated assessment rules say the narratives assessment is open-book, but they do not state that a resource booklet is issued in the examination room for this component (that provision is stated only for the themes component). The lesson should not assert a detail the specification does not state.
findings.correction: quote a short piece of Latin exactly as printed in the text

findings.claim: Virgil extends the darkness into an <dfn class="term" ...>extended simile</dfn> earlier in the episode, comparing the opened-up cave to the underworld itself, which makes the den feel monstrous long before the two finally meet in combat.
findings.problem: Misplaces and mis-describes the simile. In the set text (section E, Aeneid 8.233-246) the underworld comparison comes immediately BEFORE the final fight, after Hercules has already torn the rock peak off the cave, and it is prompted by daylight suddenly flooding in ('It was as if the deepest parts of the earth split apart by force, unbarred the chambers of the underworld... the spirits of the dead panicked as light was inflicted on them'), not by darkness or smoke. It is therefore neither an extension of the darkness nor 'long before' the combat.
findings.correction: Just before the final fight, Virgil compares the cave, ripped open to the daylight, to the underworld itself being unbarred, with the spirits of the dead panicking as light is forced on them — a comparison developed over several lines that makes Cacus's den feel like a pocket of the world of the dead.

findings.claim: First Cacus tries to escape by breathing out a wall of smoke and fire to blind Hercules.
findings.problem: Contradicts the set text. Section F states explicitly that no escape from danger remained for Cacus ('ille autem, neque enim fuga iam super ulla pericli') before he vomits the smoke: the smoke is a last defensive attempt to conceal himself and blind Hercules, not an escape attempt. The same wording recurs in the first practice question.
findings.correction: First, with no escape left, Cacus breathes out a wall of smoke and fire to blind Hercules and hide himself in the darkness.

findings.claim: Misreading a perfect passive participle as if it described an ongoing or present action is one of the most common ways marks are lost when explaining what a sentence actually says.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about marking behaviour and about what candidates commonly get wrong; the specification publishes no band descriptors, no examiner commentary of this kind and nothing about frequency of candidate errors.
findings.correction: Be careful not to read a perfect passive participle as if it described an ongoing or present action: it tells you the action was already complete before the time of the main verb.

findings.claim: Naming a device such as asyndeton or alliteration without saying what it achieves earns you very little credit.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about how answers are credited. The specification publishes no mark tariffs or band descriptors for this component, so no claim can be made about how much credit a bare device-name receives.
findings.correction: Naming a device such as asyndeton or alliteration is only the starting point: the question asks for the effect, so always go on to explain what the words achieve.

findings.claim: Words describing darkness and fire are placed side by side without any connecting word — an example of asyndeton
findings.problem: Loose labelling. Placing contrasting words next to each other (as in 'commixtis igne tenebris', darkness mixed with fire) is juxtaposition of opposites; asyndeton, correctly defined in the glossary, is the omission of conjunctions between items in a list or between clauses. No supporting quotation is given for the asyndeton claim.
findings.correction: Virgil sets words for fire and darkness right next to one another ('commixtis igne tenebris', 'the darkness mixed with fire'), and elsewhere in the fight he strips out connecting words between clauses — asyndeton — so that the action rushes forward at the speed of the fight itself.
